title: Probing proximity-induced superconductivity in bilayer graphene using gate-defined quantum dots
authors: Philipp Schmidt, Mathies Funke, Till Tenger, Katarina Stanojević, Hubert Dulisch, Kenji Watanabe, Takashi Taniguchi, Fabian Hassler, Christian Volk, Szabolcs Csonka, Christoph Stampfer
abstract: Van der Waals heterostructures offer a direct way of combining two-dimensional (2D) materials with different electronic properties, such as 2D semiconductors, metals, and superconductors, in a single device. Bilayer graphene (BLG) is particularly attractive in this context, as its electrically tunable band gap enables local control of tunnel barriers and quantum dots. Here, we realize an all-2D hybrid platform based on BLG proximitized by superconducting NbSe$_2$. Using local electrostatic gates, we define tunnel barriers and quantum dots at different distances from the lateral superconductor-semiconductor interface. The quantum dots serve as local spectroscopic probes of the proximitized BLG channel segment, forming tunable superconductor-quantum dot-normal conductor junction devices. Coulomb blockade and finite-bias spectroscopy reveal a proximity-induced superconducting gap of up to $80\,\mathrm{μeV}$ and allow to track its evolution with increasing distance from the NbSe$_2$ contact. We find that the local density of states remains suppressed over distances exceeding 1 $μ$m, consistent with superconducting proximity through a highly ballistic BLG channel. Our results show that BLG-superconductor hybrids offer a controllable platform where quantum dots and quantum point contacts can be well combined with superconductivity.
summary: This experiment demonstrates a highly controllable all-2D platform using bilayer graphene proximitized by a superconductor ($	ext{NbSe}_2$). By integrating gate-defined quantum dots, the researchers measured the proximity-induced superconducting gap ($\Delta^*$) and mapped its decay as a function of distance. This work establishes $	ext{BLG/NbSe}_2$ hybrids as a versatile tool for studying superconducting correlations in nanoscale electronic devices.
main_problem: The study aims to probe the proximity-induced superconducting gap in bilayer graphene (BLG) by integrating gate-defined quantum dots into a superconducting hybrid platform.
main_result: The researchers successfully measured a proximity-induced superconducting gap up to $80\,\mathrm{\mu eV}$ and mapped its decay spatially, confirming the tunability of superconducting correlations in this all-2D system.
method: Transport measurements, including Coulomb blockade and finite-bias spectroscopy, were performed on $	ext{BLG}$ patterned into quantum dots coupled to a superconducting $	ext{NbSe}_2$ region.
model_or_system: The platform is an all-2D hybrid structure combining $	ext{BLG}$ (electrostatically tunable) with superconducting $	ext{NbSe}_2$. Quantum dots act as local probes forming $	ext{S–S}^*-	ext{QD–N}$ junctions.
key_observables: Proximity-induced superconducting gap ($\Delta^*$), local density of states (LDOS) suppression, and conductance ($G$) as a function of bias voltage and gate voltages.
important_parameters: Superconducting gap magnitude ($\Delta^* \approx 80\,\mathrm{\mu eV}$), decay length ($\sim 1\,\mathrm{\mu m}$), and critical magnetic field ($B^*_c \simeq 8 	ext{ mT}$).
main_assumptions: The gap decay follows a ballistic scaling law $\Delta^*(x) \sim \pi\hbar v/(4x)$, and the system operates in a highly ballistic regime.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the device structure, the decay of the proximity gap with distance, and differential conductance measurements showing gap features and Coulomb diamonds.
paper_structure: The work systematically demonstrates the ability to create and probe superconducting proximity effects by first establishing the device geometry, then measuring the gap magnitude, and finally mapping its spatial dependence across the $	ext{BLG}$ channel.
why_interesting: The ability to electrostatically control the superconducting coupling strength and map the resulting gap spatially provides a clean platform to test theoretical models of superconducting proximity effects in 2D materials, relevant to topological superconductivity.
